<reason>Both sides were disciplined, well-grounded, and rhetorically strong, with B landing the most memorable framing ("a kit on a wall needs someone standing beside it") and winning the reach/consent clash — treatment as a chain of voluntary steps versus enforcement that acts without permission. But A won the debate's decisive sequence: A's Q1 forced B to concede that enforcement pressure "cannot transmit through price," which had been the explicit mechanism behind B's initiation-suppression and future-pool arguments (B1.7, B2.6). A's closing converted this into a clean coherence and unfalsifiability indictment (rise = "restructuring," fall = "pressure caught up"), and B's closing patch — that the concession was about A's test, not B's mechanism — was spin, since B's own case ran through price. Meanwhile A's affirmative mechanism survived intact: B never contested that medication roughly halves mortality even in a saturated fentanyl supply, and A gave a plausible regulatory path to scale. On 2024 attribution, A's step-change answer (OTC naloxone, settlement funds) plus the unanswered east-to-west geographic gradient at least neutralized B's inflection-point argument. B's strong frame could not substitute for a market mechanism B itself had hollowed out.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Q1 price-mechanism challenge, B's concession in B4.1 that pressure cannot transmit through price, and A's closing exploitation of that concession as the load-bearing beam of B's entire case — the cleanest and most damaging exchange in the debate.</best_rebuttal>
